title: The Fate of Crystalline Topological Phenomena in the Continuum
abstract: The continuum limit is a widely used theoretical construct for obtaining continuum field-theories of crystalline systems. We study the formulation of a continuum limit for gapped bosonic phases and ask whether their topological properties survive passage to the continuum. Using methods in algebraic topology and category theory, we give a rigorous formulation of the continuum limit and construct a surjective global map relating crystalline topological phases across all finite point-group symmetries to continuum invertible topological phases. Consequently, we find that some lattice phases admit no continuum limit, while distinct lattice phases that do admit a continuum limit can share the same continuum image, hence implying that some lattice topological data can collapse. Conversely, we find that every continuum invertible phase admits a faithful crystalline realization. In addition to the general framework, we apply it to several examples, including studies of a 2D rotation-symmetric phase, higher-order topological phases, and the mixed spin-lattice anomaly of the deconfined quantum critical point between an antiferromagnet and valence bond solid.
summary: The paper rigorously analyzes the passage from crystalline topological phases on a lattice to their corresponding continuum field theories. Using advanced algebraic topology, it proves that while every continuum phase can be realized on a lattice, the process loses information, meaning distinct lattice configurations can map to the same continuous description.
main_problem: The central problem is rigorously determining whether the topological properties of gapped bosonic systems defined on a discrete lattice (crystalline phases) survive when taking the continuum limit to form a field theory.
main_result: The map from crystalline to continuum topological phases is surjective, meaning every continuum phase has a lattice realization; however, it is generally not injective, implying that some microscopic lattice information collapses in the continuum description.
method: The authors employ advanced mathematical tools, including algebraic topology and category theory, to construct a rigorous stratification map relating crystalline classification groups ($\Theta^{d+1}(BG)$) to continuum ones ($\Theta^{d+1}(	ext{BO}(d))$).
model_or_system: The study focuses on gapped bosonic phases of matter characterized by finite point-group symmetries ($G \subset O(d)$), analyzing the relationship between lattice topological invariants and their effective low-energy continuum field theories.
key_observables: Topological invariants, such as those classified by group cohomology ($\Theta^{d+1}(BG)$) and cobordism theory ($\Omega_{d+1}^O(BG)$).
important_parameters: The analysis is restricted to point-group symmetries ($G \subset O(d)$), deliberately excluding lattice translations, and focuses specifically on the 2-primary torsion sector of the classification groups.
main_assumptions: The work assumes gapped phases and restricts attention to bosonic systems whose continuum limit TQFTs are assumed to be diffeomorphism-invariant (excluding certain metric dependencies).
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates a surjective 'funnel' mapping the classification of crystalline SPTs onto the continuum SPT classification.
paper_structure: The paper develops the mathematical framework by defining the map between lattice and continuum classifications, proving its surjectivity, analyzing the loss of information (non-injectivity), and applying this general theory to specific physical examples like 2D rotation-symmetric phases and quantum critical points.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous mathematical framework for understanding how microscopic symmetries and lattice details constrain macroscopic continuum descriptions in topological materials, which is crucial for designing novel quantum states.
